taking-over-a-state-or-town.essay:
This route starts from something that already exists. Instead of looking for empty water or unclaimed rock, a group tries to take over a government that is already running, either a country's or a town's. The land stays where it is, owned and governed by the same existing country or local government. There are two very different ways to try this. One is to move people in and vote. The other is armed force, usually by mercenaries, meaning soldiers for hire.

A town is a unit of local government. It gets its powers from the state or country around it, and those powers cover local matters such as the town budget, local services and, in many places, the use of land. Moving to a town and voting there is ordinary legal behaviour. Suppose a few hundred people move into a town of about a thousand and elect a majority of its council. They can then cut the budget and change local rules. The next morning, state law, national law, the courts and the tax office apply as they did before. Voters and courts in a town can only change what local government controls, and a council has no power over criminal law, passports or the country's borders.

The first bump is getting enough people to come. The Free State Project, a plan for libertarians (people who favour very limited government) to move to New Hampshire, began in 2001 with an article by Jason Sorens that proposed an independent libertarian nation or, failing that, concessions from the US government. Sorens calculated that 20,000 people moving to one small state could change it. Pledges reached 20,000 on 3 February 2016, and by May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. In the 2017 to 2018 term, Free Staters held 17 of the 400 seats in the state House of Representatives. A movement called NH Exit Now, formed in 2026, calls for secession, and New Hampshire remains a US state. In Texas v. White in 1869 the US Supreme Court held that a state cannot secede on its own, with no way out "except through revolution or through consent of the States".

The second bump is daily life and cost. A smaller attempt, the Free Town Project, began in 2004 when a splinter group chose Grafton, New Hampshire, for its lack of zoning laws (rules on how land may be used) and its very low property tax. No records were kept of how many came. The population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all the newcomers men, many living in yurts, trailers, tents and shipping containers. They voted through a 30% cut in the small town budget and removed funding for the county's senior citizens' council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs.

The third bump is the neighbours, and then the higher authorities. The largest case is Rajneeshpuram in Oregon. In 1981 followers of the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch for $5.75 million and within three years had built a city of up to about 7,000 people. The nearest town, Antelope, had under 60 people. Its residents voted in April 1982 on dissolving the town to avoid a takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat the plan. In May 1982 the ranch voted to become a city. Oregon's attorney general argued that the new city merged church and state, and a land-use group argued that it broke land-use law. Federal Judge Helen Frye ruled against the city in the church-and-state suit in late 1985, too late to matter, and that ruling was not contested. The Oregon Court of Appeals ruled in 1986 that the incorporation had not broken the state's agricultural land goals, and the Oregon Supreme Court closed the litigation in 1987, which left the city vacant and bankrupt but legal under Oregon law.

Criminal cases brought the project down before those lawsuits were settled. In 1984 some leaders deliberately spread disease to lower turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and sending 45 to hospital, and a plot to kill the US attorney for Oregon followed. Rajneesh, accused of immigration violations, entered a plea without admitting guilt and agreed to leave the country. The commune broke up in 1985.

Armed takeover is a crime in the places involved, and foreign governments, police and informers have usually stopped it early. The first obstacle is money. For the 1981 attempt in Seychelles, an island country in the Indian Ocean, the mercenary Mike Hoare advised raising $5 million, and $300,000 was found. The second is secrecy, because people must be hired and weapons moved. In Operation Red Dog, a 1981 plot by white supremacists against Dominica in the Caribbean, about $70,000 was collected, and the replacement boat captain, Michael Howell, went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. On 27 April 1981 nine men were arrested at a New Orleans marina as they prepared to board, with three undercover agents in the group. US law punishes preparing, from within the United States, a military expedition against a country at peace with it, with up to three years in prison (18 USC 960). In Seychelles, a security officer at the airport found an AK-47 in the bag of one of the 53 men.

The third is the law of every country along the way. After the Seychelles gunfight, most of the mercenaries hijacked an Air India airliner to Durban. South Africa, which had encouraged the plot, charged them under its aviation law over the hijacking and not over the coup attempt, and 34 served about four months. Hoare himself got ten years and was released in May 1985 under an amnesty, after about three. Seychelles sentenced four captured men to death, and all six prisoners were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment. In the Wonga Coup of 2004 against Equatorial Guinea, police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 with 64 former soldiers and arrested Simon Mann, who served three years in Zimbabwe and was then sentenced in Equatorial Guinea to more than 34 years, until a pardon in 2009.

Bob Denard is often taken as proof that this works. He landed in the Comoros in 1978 with 43 men, overthrew Ali Soilih and for 11 years ran a 500-strong presidential guard under President Abdallah. He held power through a recognised president and founded nothing new, and witnesses at his later trial said French intelligence had supported him. After Abdallah was shot in 1989 Denard left, and when he landed again in 1995 the French army ended the attempt within about a week. A French court later convicted him. He is the one long-lasting case, and his control ended as well.

South Africa's apartheid government declared four homelands, or Bantustans, independent between 1976 and 1981, after the Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 made every Black South African a citizen of one, while saying they stayed South African citizens for purposes of international law. No other government recognised them, so a government's own declaration settled nothing abroad, and they were absorbed back in 1994. Slab City in California, a camp of about 4,000 people in winter and 150 in summer on a former Marine base, has no local government, but California and US law still apply, though they are largely not enforced there.

The most workable version is the open one, and Marinaleda in Spain is its longest example. Landless farm workers there formed the Workers' Unity Collective, won 9 of 11 council seats in 1979 and kept the same mayor until 2023. After a hunger strike in 1980 and a 30-day occupation in 1984, 1,200 hectares of a duke's farm were handed over for local use in 1991. Critics say almost 66% of its income comes from higher levels of government. It remains an ordinary Spanish municipality under Spanish law. The voting route can win local offices and change how a place lives, for as long as the voters stay and the laws above allow it, and final authority stays where it was. Recognition as a new country by this route is close to nil.

indigenous-prior-sovereignty.essay:
Many countries were formed on land where other peoples already lived and governed themselves. Those peoples, called Indigenous peoples, often say that their authority is older than the country and that they never gave it up. The country usually treats the matter as a domestic one, to be settled under its own law. Each side begins from a different starting point, and the courts that decide most disputes belong to the country.

This route is open only to a people with an existing claim, one that comes from a long history on the land. A new founder cannot acquire it by moving somewhere, joining a group or buying property. The real gains have come through negotiated land claims, court rulings and long use of a document, and each result stays within the existing country. That explains why self-rule here can grow a good deal while recognition as a separate state stays close to nil.

To see how the law came to this point, it helps to go back to the rule that European powers brought with them. In Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, the United States Supreme Court considered a land purchase from the Piankeshaw people. Chief Justice John Marshall set out the doctrine of discovery, under which a European power gained sovereignty (the right to rule) over land it discovered, along with the sole right to buy out the Indigenous occupants, who kept only a right to occupy it. The case is still taught and is the basis of the American law of aboriginal title, the rights Indigenous peoples keep over their land. In 1831, in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, he described Indian tribes as "domestic dependent nations", and in Worcester v. Georgia in 1832 he held a Georgia law on Cherokee land void. So in US courts the country holds final authority, and the argument is over how much it left in place.

Courts can still give large results within that frame. McGirt v. Oklahoma, decided in 2020, is the leading example. In the 19th century Congress set aside land for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation as a reservation. The question was whether the reservation ended when Oklahoma became a state. By 5 to 4, in an opinion by Justice Neil Gorsuch, the court held that Congress had never ended it, so the land is still Indian country, the legal term for land under tribal and federal authority. Under the Major Crimes Act, a federal law on serious crimes, Oklahoma could not prosecute Native Americans for the listed crimes there. A state appeals court applied the same reasoning to nine other nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country.

In 2021 the state appeals court ruled that McGirt did not apply to old convictions, and the US Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to that ruling. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court held that the state shares with the federal government the power to prosecute crimes by non-Native people against Native victims there. A later case can narrow an earlier win. McGirt also concerned who may prosecute crimes on the land and did not make the nations independent states.

International law offers a statement of principle. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted by the General Assembly on 13 September 2007, says in Article 3 that these peoples have the right to self-determination and in Article 4 the right to autonomy or self-government in internal and local affairs. Article 46 says nothing in it authorises action that would dismember or impair the territorial integrity of sovereign states. It is a resolution and does not bind countries as a treaty does. Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States voted against, and each later endorsed it in some form.

Negotiation has produced the largest result on the ground. Nunavut, in the Canadian Arctic, covers 2,093,190 square kilometres and had 36,858 people in 2021, of whom 84 percent were Inuit. Inuit organisations and the federal government began discussing a split of the Northwest Territories in 1976. Residents backed division in a vote in 1982, and the land-claims agreement was completed in September 1992 and ratified by nearly 85 percent of voters. Parliament passed the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act in 1993, and the territory began on 1 April 1999. A 2024 agreement gives its government control over its land and resources. From the first talks to the first day of the territory took 23 years, and Nunavut is a territory of Canada that makes no claim to be a state.

Elected bodies inside a country are another form. The Sámi, an Indigenous people of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, elect parliaments in three of those countries, opened in 1989, 1993 and 1996, and Sweden's must follow decisions of the national parliament. In Russia, as of 2017, the authorities did not recognise the Kola Sámi Assembly as a lawmaking body. None of these bodies claims independence.

Documents show what happens at a border. The Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, have issued their own passport since at least 1923, when one went to the Cayuga statesman Deskaheh for a trip to the League of Nations. Other countries decide case by case. In July 2010 Britain refused it for the Haudenosaunee lacrosse team, which turned down an American offer of US passports. Israel accepted the team's passports in 2018, subject to Canadian assurances that they could return, and Ireland accepted them in 2022. The European Union lists it as a fantasy passport, and it is not accepted for entry into Canada. Countries decide whether to accept the passport, recognise the government or pass the law.

Conflict with a country can last far longer than one government. The Kīngitanga, the Māori King Movement in New Zealand, began in 1858 as a rival authority. Troops crossed into the Waikato region in July 1863 and the government confiscated 486,500 hectares. The movement continues, and its monarch is not recognised in New Zealand law or by many tribes. In 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal, which hears Māori claims against the Crown, concluded that the chiefs who signed the Māori text of the 1840 treaty did not give up sovereignty, which leaves open how and when the Crown gained it.

Unity among the people concerned is often the hardest bump. The Hawaiian sovereignty movement traces its case to the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, and in 1993 Congress passed an Apology Resolution acknowledging that the overthrow was illegal. In Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs in 2009, a unanimous US Supreme Court held that the resolution's "whereas" clauses did not change the state's rights and obligations over the ceded lands of the former kingdom. The groups differ on what should follow. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi reported 21,000 members in 1997, the Nation of Hawaiʻi wants a republic, and many groups opposed the Akaka Bill, which would have begun federal recognition. Justice Anthony Kennedy halted a 2015 vote count for a planned convention. In 2007 the Republic of Lakotah, led by Russell Means, announced withdrawal from old treaties. Recognised Lakota tribal governments had not backed it, and a federal official said the withdrawal did not mean anything.

A silent government has not agreed to anything, and in Australia the courts have closed the question from the other side. In Coe v. Commonwealth in 1993, Chief Justice Mason of the High Court struck out a claim of Aboriginal sovereignty, writing that the Mabo decision of 1992 is entirely at odds with the idea that sovereignty adverse to the Crown lies with the Aboriginal people, and that the Crown's sovereignty cannot be challenged in Australian courts. The Murrawarri people in Australia declared independence in 2013 and asked the Crown to produce a treaty, a deed of cession or a declaration of war by a deadline. The Crown did not reply, and the council took silence as confirmation, but the government has not acknowledged the republic, and it uses Australian money.

The most workable version is a recognised people negotiating with the country, backed by a court case or a strong historical record, for land, money and powers written into law. It takes decades, it depends on the people concerned acting together, and it delivers self-rule inside the existing state. Nothing in these cases has yet produced a new country that others recognise, and a person with no such claim has no way to use this route.

exile-and-landless-authority.essay:
A government in exile is a body that claims the right to govern a place while operating from another country. Someone else holds the land. The exile body holds a claim, a community of supporters and whatever standing other governments choose to give it. It helps to picture an office, a set of elected officials and a list of members, all located in a foreign city and all concerned with a homeland they cannot enter or do not control.

This arrangement is different from a micronation, a self-declared small country. A government in exile normally grows out of a real political event at home, such as a flight from an invasion or a declaration of independence that was overrun. The claim therefore rests on a history that many people recognise, and it has a population that cares about it. A person starting from nothing has none of that, and an office abroad with a flag would have the legal standing of a private club.

The law here begins with a question that is not fully settled, which is what makes a state. One view, called the constitutive theory, says a state exists only when others recognise it. The other, the declarative theory, says recognition is not required if the tests in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty defining a state, are met. Those tests are a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries. Article 3 of that convention takes the second side, saying a state's political existence does not depend on recognition, and what governments actually do typically falls somewhere between the two. A body in exile has trouble under both. Under the first, it depends on others agreeing. Under the second, it does not control the territory it names. The country in control simply keeps the territory, and neither theory gives the exile body any way to remove it.

The longest-running examples show what can be done anyway. The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic declared independence in Minsk on 25 March 1918, during the German occupation in the First World War, and Germany did not officially recognise it, though it had diplomatic contacts with neighbours such as Finland and the Baltic states. It left Minsk as Bolshevik armies advanced at the end of 1918 and has been in exile since 1919, and as of 2026 it is described as the oldest existing government in exile. A Red Army advance in 1945 forced it to move again, to western Germany. Today it works as an advocacy group among Belarusians in North America, Britain and elsewhere. It says it holds a symbolic mandate that it wants to hand to a democratically elected Belarusian parliament.

The Tibetan case is the fullest working model. In March 1959, as he fled to India, the 14th Dalai Lama, then Tibet's head of government, rejected the 1951 Seventeen Point Agreement with China, and on 29 April he re-established his cabinet in exile. The Central Tibetan Administration, based in Dharamshala in northern India, now has courts, a parliament and an executive under the Charter of the Tibetans in Exile, adopted in 1991 and amended in 2011. That year the Dalai Lama gave up his political duties and executive power passed to an elected leader called the Sikyong. Penpa Tsering was sworn in for a second five-year term in May 2026.

Suppose a community wants to run something like this. The first problem is the host. The body must sit in some country, and that country decides how much activity it allows. It can allow offices, meetings and elections, and it can stop them, since the host's law applies on its soil. Many hosts have reasons to be careful, because the government at home may object. The Tibetan administration operates by India's tolerance.

The second problem is money. An exile body has no territory to tax, and it cannot compel payment. Tibetans abroad make yearly contributions recorded in the Green Book, a document sometimes called a passport, and funding comes mainly from these contributions, private donations and aid from governments such as India and the United States. That aid is given for welfare work, and receiving it does not amount to recognition. No country recognises the administration as a sovereign government, meaning one with the legal right to rule Tibet.

The third problem is keeping people. Voters are scattered, children grow up as citizens of other countries, and each generation must choose to stay involved. Members stay under the law of wherever they live for tax, marriage, inheritance, police and courts. The exile body's papers may have value inside the community, but they do not replace a national passport. The Green Book is sometimes called a passport, and that name does not make it one.

The fourth is pressure from home. Members with relatives or interests in the homeland are exposed there. In June 2023 the Belarusian KGB declared the Rada an extremist group.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic shows how far standing can go when territory and diplomacy are added. The Polisario Front proclaimed it on 27 February 1976 after Spain left Western Sahara. It claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000 east of a 2,700-kilometre sand wall built by Morocco, a share given as anywhere from a fifth to 30%. Daily government runs from the Rabuni camp in Tindouf, Algeria, and the camps there held about 173,600 people by a 2023 estimate. It is a full member of the African Union, and counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members. Recognition can also be taken back. Many countries have withdrawn or suspended it, the United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020, and in 2026 Mali said it was withdrawing recognition. A referendum promised in 1991 never took place because the two sides dispute who may vote, and on 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted, with 11 in favour, for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan.

Exile can end in a return, when the government at home changes. Poland's government left the country in September 1939 and sat in London from 1940. France withdrew recognition on 29 June 1945, the United States and Britain on 5 July, and the Holy See last, in 1972. On 22 December 1990 the last exile president, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed the state symbols to Lech Wałęsa in Warsaw.

Some common ideas do not survive these cases. An exile government does not become a state through age, since the Rada has more than a century behind it and holds no territory. A good internal record does not bring recognition either, as the Tibetan elections show. It is also a mistake to assume that having no land removes all risk. A state has little to seize once a host allows the body to operate, so such bodies tend to last, but the host can change its mind and the home state can act against members.

The most workable version is a modest one. A real community abroad runs elections, keeps a membership roll, collects voluntary contributions and speaks for its homeland to foreign governments, in a host country that tolerates it. The Tibetan and Belarusian cases show this can last for decades. Its limits are clear in the same cases. It gains no territory by its own efforts, it depends on a host, and whether other governments deal with it is their decision.

no-territory-conceptual.essay:
Some declared countries exist only as an idea, an artwork or an organisation. Nothing is claimed on the ground, or the claim is carried with a person or an object. People do this for several reasons, including protest, art, religion, study and amusement. The law's response is simple, because nothing happens to the legal position of anyone involved. Nothing is owned, and the people remain under the law of the place where they stand.

To see why, it helps to know what a state is in law. The usual checklist comes from the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, which asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries. A conceptual country has no population living in a place under its rule and no territory. Its government governs only those who agree to it, and other countries do not deal with it as a state. There is no treaty, office or court that a declaration needs to pass through, so anyone can make one and no authority needs to refuse it. Nobody has to raid a place that does not exist, which is why these projects tend to survive for a long time, and also why governments do not trouble to answer them.

Two real situations come close, and they show what the law actually asks. The Sovereign Order of Malta, a Catholic order, has no national territory and is still treated as a sovereign entity under international law. It keeps diplomatic relations with about 115 states, signs treaties and has been an observer at the UN General Assembly since 1994. That standing comes from centuries of history and from governments choosing to deal with it, and a new group cannot declare its way into it. The other situation concerns states losing land. In its climate opinion of July 2025, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Low-lying island states pressed this point because of rising seas. The sentence protects a state that already exists, it did not mention sea level rise in terms, and how far it reaches is still argued by scholars. It gives nothing to a project that never was a state.

The best-known example is Nutopia, announced by John Lennon and Yoko Ono at a New York press conference on 2 April 1973. Its declaration says it has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Anyone could become a citizen by declaring awareness of it. Its flag was a white handkerchief, and its anthem is four seconds of silence. There was a practical side. Lennon had just received an order to leave the United States, and all citizens were to be ambassadors, with a request for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection foreign diplomats have from a host country's courts, and for recognition by the United Nations. No government is known to have granted the immunity. His home-country problem was solved by ordinary US immigration law, when the deportation order was overturned in 1975 and he received a green card in 1976.

That case shows the first and most common misunderstanding. A declaration does not reach the legal problem the person already has. Immunity comes from an agreement between a receiving state and a sending state, so naming yourself an ambassador has no effect on a court or an immigration officer. Your home country's law continues to apply to your income, your debts, your marriage and any charge against you.

The cases differ in how seriously they organise. Nova Roma, formed in 1998 and later incorporated in the US state of Maine, aims to restore the religion, culture and values of ancient Rome. It calls itself a sovereign nation and has a senate, elected officials and laws passed by members' votes, with Latin as its official language. It minted coins in 2000 and 2005. Its most recent dated activity is a twentieth-anniversary celebration in Rome, and what it does now has not been confirmed. The Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia, founded in 2015 by Karo Yagjian, is a feminist micronation and art project whose territory is two book-sized slabs of obsidian, a volcanic glass, carried in a briefcase usually based in Oakland, California. Huck magazine estimated about 250 citizens in 2021, roughly 50 with passports. Its present activity has not been confirmed. The obsidian itself is personal property under the law of wherever the briefcase is.

Passports are the first real pitfall. Printing a booklet for fun is one thing, but using it at a border is another. Border officers check documents against lists of real issuers, and a document from an unrecognised body is at best refused. Members who treat one as real can face questions or charges, so the sensible use of such a passport is as a keepsake. A real passport stays necessary for every actual trip.

Money comes next, and it is where a harmless project can turn into a legal problem. Selling coins, stamps and certificates as souvenirs is ordinary trade, and the seller owes ordinary tax. Atlantium, founded in Sydney in 1981 by three teenagers, sold coins, stamps and banknotes in its imperial solidus and had almost 3,000 citizens as of 2015, most of whom signed up online and never visited. Selling titles or promises of future value raises other questions. The Global Country of World Peace, launched by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi on 7 October 2000 and incorporated in Iowa in 2002, is run by initiates called rajas, and reports say that title cost $1 million or more. It also issued a currency, the raam, accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands.

The same group shows what happens when a project of this kind goes looking for land under its own authority. It offered Suriname $1.3 billion over three years for a 200-year lease of 3,500 acres, and no deal followed. Tuvalu rejected a proposed city-state in 2001, and Rota in the Northern Mariana Islands declined a request for 100 acres in 2002. Costa Rica expelled its representative in 2002 after officials said to be acting for the group allegedly offered Talamanca families payments to appoint a king. It did buy ordinary private property, including a 30-acre island in Ireland and more than 1,000 acres in Kansas, all of it under the law of the country concerned.

Land also does not change the legal position when a project buys it privately. Slowjamastan is a patch of California desert that the DJ Randy Williams bought in 2021, 11.07 acres for $19,000, and declared independent that December. More than 25,000 citizens had applied online by March 2026, while nobody lived there as of February 2025. Williams cites the Montevideo Convention as the basis of its legitimacy, and the convention's tests do not make a declaration effective on their own, since other countries must still be willing to deal with it. The project has no legal recognition. Atlantium's plots in Australia likewise stay under Australian law.

Another misunderstanding is that a long life or a large roll means growing legal status. Several of these projects have lasted decades as organisations, and Nutopia has taken citizens through a website since April 2024. None is reported to have gained recognition from any country.

The most workable version is exactly what it appears to be. It is an artwork, a society or a nonprofit that openly calls its country an idea, registers as a normal organisation if it holds money, pays ordinary taxes on sales and never asks anyone to rely on its documents. It can carry a message for decades at very little cost, and it carries little risk as long as no one is misled. The limit is that it gives its members no legal protection, tax status, travel right or land, because nothing in law has changed.

inland-waters.essay:
An island in a lake or river can seem to sit between countries, especially on a border. The water around it belongs to the countries on its shores, and a newcomer gets no share. The ocean has a stretch that belongs to no one, the high seas. Lakes and rivers have nothing equivalent, because land under some country's control encloses them.

To understand how these borders work, start with a river. When two countries agree that a river is their border, they usually sign a treaty. A treaty that names only the river normally means the line follows the thalweg, the deepest channel, since that is the part boats use. Rivers shift and split, though, so the treaty may fail to say which channel it meant. Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 km² in the Chobe River that floods for several months each year. An 1890 treaty between Germany and Britain put the line in the "main channel" without saying which one. In 1996 Botswana and Namibia asked the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, to decide. In 1999 it studied the river and held that the northern channel was the main one, so the island fell on the Botswana side. Nobody lives there permanently, and it is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area. The case asked only which of the two countries held the island.

Lakes work the same way, with lines drawn by treaty or by old colonial orders. Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 m² in Lake Victoria, valued for the Nile perch in the waters around it. A colonial order, the Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council of 1926, draws the Kenya-Uganda line across the lake by straight lines between named islands, and it is copied into the Ugandan constitution. Two Kenyan fishermen say they settled the rock in 1991, a Ugandan fisherman says he arrived in 2004, and Kenya says Ugandan marine police raised a flag in June 2004. In February 2009 Kenyans there were told to buy special Ugandan permits. By then the rock held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino, with 131 people reported, while Ugandan police estimated about 500. Ministers agreed that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers, and they stayed. A 2009 survey placed the rock 510 metres on the Kenyan side, and its report was still unpublished in January 2025. Wikipedia says the results were announced and Uganda withdrew, while a Kenya News Agency report says surveyors disagreed and the joint work stopped. In January 2025 residents petitioned Kenya's president over harassment by Ugandan police, and that August fishermen said Ugandan officials were still seizing their gear. Settling first or raising a flag did not decide the matter.

Some waters have no agreed line at all. Lake Constance, where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet, has no binding agreement fixing the borders in its deep part. Areas under 25 metres deep go to the nearest country, and shipping and fishing have treaties of their own. Switzerland holds that the line runs down the middle. Austria says the deep part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement called a condominium, meaning shared rule. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous. Under every one of those views, the deep water belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so an outsider has no claim.

The Caspian Sea, at 389,000 km², is the largest case. Its five shore countries argued for decades over whether it counts as a sea or a lake, because the law of the sea applies only to seas. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea was signed on 12 August 2018 at Aktau, Kazakhstan. It would give each shore country 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water and a further 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface would be a common space open to the five members, and the seabed is left to agreements between the countries concerned. It was not in force as of September 2026, because all five must ratify it, meaning formally approve it. Four have. Iran's cabinet approved it on 22 July 2026 and sent it to parliament, which had not ratified it. Even the open middle is for the five named countries, so an outsider has none of the freedoms found on the ocean. Iranian patrol boats have at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed oil fields.

A treaty can also give an island to two countries at once. Pheasant Island, in the Bidasoa river, stays a condominium of France and Spain under the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659, and each governs it for six months in turn. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres. It is uninhabited and eroding, and access is forbidden apart from rare heritage days. Naval personnel check it every five days.

A river island can also be overlooked for a time. Ada Kaleh, in the Danube, was forgotten at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and stayed Ottoman in law, with other countries on both banks. Its residents paid no tax or customs and were not drafted, and it became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest. Austria-Hungary declared sovereignty in 1913, Romania occupied it in 1919, and the Treaty of Lausanne, which the residents did not sign, made it Romanian in 1923. In 1970 the Iron Gates dam flooded it. Ada Kaleh had a legal owner throughout, and its residents had no say in the treaty or the dam.

New land raises a fresher problem. Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, with about 3,000 people under Peruvian administration. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made it a district of its Loreto region. Colombia's president said in August that Peru had "appropriated it by law". Colombia argues that the island had not formed when the 1922 and 1929 treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. Peru treats it as an extension of an older island. Land that a river newly creates may fall outside a treaty's words, and the competition for it still runs between the neighbouring countries. The Chamizal dispute between the United States and Mexico shows a rule used for moving rivers. An 1884 treaty accepted that a river border moves with the river only when the change is gradual, and that a sudden shift leaves the border where it was. The Rio Grande shifted at El Paso, a 1911 tribunal recommended splitting the land, and the United States rejected that. A treaty signed in 1963 largely followed the recommendation, and the land passed to Mexico in October 1967, with more than 5,600 residents of El Paso displaced. Whether anything like that rule decides Santa Rosa depends on the words of the 1922 and 1929 treaties, which Colombia and Peru read differently.

Suppose a group floats a platform onto a large lake and declares a state. Lake police and customs officers from the nearest shore are a short boat ride away, and they are the practical limit. Every supply run ends at a dock in one of the shore countries. There is no high-seas freedom to argue from. Banks, tax, courts and building permits are those of the shore country.

The common misunderstanding treats a gap in a line as a gap in ownership. A border argument, a missing treaty, a shifting channel and a forgotten island have each been resolved or left open among the countries on the shore.

The most workable version is ordinary. A floating home, lodge or tourist concession can be built on lakes and rivers with the permission of the country that holds the spot, under that country's law. Building is easier than at sea, and supply and medical care are close. It gives no new status, since it is one more property in an existing country, and on a contested border it may bring officials from two countries, as on Migingo.

buffer-zones.essay:
When two armies stop fighting, they often agree to pull back from each other and leave a strip of land between them, so that a stray shot or a patrol does not restart the war. That strip is a buffer zone. Because no army is meant to hold it, it can look on a map like land that belongs to nobody, and people interested in empty places sometimes wonder whether a new territory could be set up there. It cannot, and the reasons say a good deal about how ceasefires work. The surrounding countries, or the parties to the ceasefire, keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or a ceasefire body controls entry. The strip is an arrangement between the two sides, and the land inside still belongs to someone in law.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone is the most guarded example. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953. Under it, each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, leaving a zone about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. Only two villages are allowed to remain inside. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side, governed and protected by the United Nations Command. It had 218 people in 2008, descended from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens and do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side. Only North Korea or the UN Command can give access. In January 2026 the UN Command strongly opposed South Korean bills that would give Seoul authority over non-military entry, calling them completely at odds with the armistice and stressing its role as the zone's administrator. If South Korea's own lawmakers meet that response, a private founder has little room. Those villagers' special position comes from the armistice and from their families' earlier ownership of the land. A newcomer has no route in, and the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world.

The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, also called the Green Line, shows a much more lived-in version. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and split the island. It runs 180 kilometres across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, ranging from under 20 metres wide in places to over 7 kilometres, and it cuts through the capital, Nicosia. The UN force in Cyprus patrols it. About 10,000 people live and farm in villages inside it, including Deneia, Athienou and Troulloi. Pyla is the only village, by the UN force's account, where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. The UN divides the zone into two kinds of ground. In the Civil Use Areas, which include these villages, people may enter freely. Everywhere else, civilian activity needs specific authorisation from the UN force, which weighs security, ownership and its own operations when dealing with civilian building. It handles about 1,000 incidents a year. These are people who were already there, or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing country. Crossing was very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased its restrictions after nearly 30 years.

A person might assume that such a mixed village, in a place neither side fully governs, would be a good place to declare something new. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state in the zone, and small events show how closely the ground is watched. In 2009 UN troops stopped villagers in Mammari, a Civil Use Area, from gathering wild asparagus in nearby fields, saying the fields were in a restricted area near Turkish military outposts. Access to restricted ground required a request to the UN. In August 2023 de facto Turkish security forces attacked UN peacekeepers near Pyla in a dispute over unauthorised construction, seriously injuring three, and the Security Council called it a violation of the status quo, meaning the existing situation that is meant to stay unchanged. In 1996 two Greek Cypriot protesters were killed during protests against the division, one beaten and one shot while climbing a flagpole. A newcomer's building or flag would land in that setting, and it would need authorisation from a force whose job is to prevent changes.

The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is a different kind of no-go strip. It was emptied because of radiation, with no army line involved. The 30-kilometre zone in Ukraine and Belarus was evacuated after the 1986 nuclear disaster, about 100,000 people in all. About 1,200 people returned in 1986. They are called samosely, meaning self-settlers. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster. Many had been told they could go home in a few days, and they then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. Some outsiders came too. Ukraine's government has not legalised their settlements, because living in the zone remains prohibited. A bill backed by Ukraine's parliament at first reading in July 2021 proposed fines of 17,000 to 42,500 hryvnia or restriction of freedom for illegal entry, and whether it passed in that form is not known. A minister said in 2013 that they receive full social support, and local officials have unofficially let elderly settlers stay.

The samosely show what tolerance looks like. Officials look away because the people are old, few and doing no harm, and because the state already pays them social support. They depend on the same state for help, which leaves them far from independent. Their number has fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017, and a Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. None of them has declared a separate state, and they remain residents of the countries that run the zone.

Several misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a ceasefire strip is a gap in sovereignty, the legal right to rule a place. A ceasefire only pauses a fight, and the claims remain in place on both sides. The UN General Assembly's Friendly Relations Declaration of 1970 says this in its own way. States must not use force to violate international lines of demarcation such as armistice lines, and that duty does not affect the parties' positions on the status of those lines. Another is that peacekeepers are a kind of government that could be persuaded to let a project go ahead. Their job is to keep the two sides apart under the terms given to them, and they have no power to give away land. A third is that a place with no tax, like the Korean village, is free of the state. Its residents hold those exemptions because of special rules from an armistice, and they are still South Korean citizens. A fourth is that physical emptiness means legal emptiness. Chernobyl has been sealed for 40 years, and two governments still run it.

The risks of trying are serious. In the Korean zone, entry without permission means walking into a military frontier. In Cyprus, unauthorised activity outside the Civil Use Areas meets UN patrols, and the 2023 clash at Pyla shows how quickly construction can involve armed forces. At Chernobyl, living in the zone is prohibited, and the radiation that emptied it remains a health issue for anyone new.

There is no way to set up a self-governing territory here. The realistic options are to study or visit where that is allowed, and to work with those trying to reduce tension, such as the bicommunal life of Pyla. People do live in these zones, under peacekeepers or military authorities, and that leaves no room for a new government. For that reason the chances of building something are put at about 10 percent, law and holding at the same low level, and recognition at a tenth of a percent. Nothing in the known record gives a legal basis for self-rule in such a place.
